intro: Angels are everywhere in modern life: on greeting cards, in movies, on holiday trees and in everyday sayings. Most of those pictures come from centuries of art and tradition. This unit goes back to the texts themselves. You will read what the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament and other ancient Jewish writings actually say about the beings they call angels, cherubim, seraphim, watchers and holy ones.

Your main guide is Michael S. Heiser (1963-2023), a scholar of the Hebrew Bible and ancient Semitic languages. In his book Angels (2018) he argued that many of the Bible's terms describe a being's role, such as messenger, while others describe its status or home, such as elohim. You will test that idea against real passages. Where other readers see things differently, you will hear their views too.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain the main words for heavenly beings and where they appear. You will be able to tell what a text says from what later writers and artists added. You will also be able to explain why the texts insist that angels serve God and are never to be worshiped, and how different traditions read those texts.
bigQuestion: What do the ancient texts really say about angels, and how can a careful reader tell that apart from what later traditions added?

timeline.t: Isaiah dates his vision of the seraphim to the year King Uzziah died
Work begins in Alexandria on the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Torah
The book of Tobit, with the angel Raphael, is likely written
Copies of the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice are made; some are later hidden near Qumran
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, which mentions the voice of the archangel
The letter to the Hebrews argues that the Son is greater than the angels
Revelation is commonly dated; in it an angel twice tells John to worship God
Pseudo-Dionysius writes The Celestial Hierarchy, with nine orders of angels
Raphael paints the Sistine Madonna, with its famous winged children
Handel composes Messiah, setting the angels' song from Luke 2:14
Michael Heiser publishes Angels: What the Bible Really Says About God's Heavenly Host

test.q: Heiser argued that the word angel describes what?
choices: A being's role as a messenger
test.why: Mal'ak and angelos mean messenger. Heiser treated angel as a role word, a job description.

test.q: Which Hebrew word can name the God of Israel and the members of his council?
test.why: Psalm 82:1 uses elohim for both. Heiser read it as a word for beings of the spirit world.

test.q: In which book does Nebuchadnezzar dream of a watcher and a holy one?
test.why: Daniel 4:13 and 4:17 describe the watchers and holy ones in the king's dream.

test.q: What do the cherubim do in Genesis 3:24 and Exodus 25?
choices: Guard the space where God is present
test.why: Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life and cover the ark, where God meets Moses.

test.q: Which beings have six wings in Isaiah 6?
test.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

test.q: Where does the idea of nine ranked choirs of angels come from?
choices: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
test.why: Pseudo-Dionysius arranged nine orders about 500 CE. Paul names some powers without ranking them.

test.q: Which two angels are named in the Protestant Bible?
test.why: Only Michael and Gabriel are named in the Protestant Bible. Raphael appears in Tobit.

test.q: Which verse lists angels and the spirits of just men as separate groups?
test.why: Hebrews 12:22-23 names the company of angels and the spirits of just men side by side.

test.q: Hebrews 1:6 quotes a line about angels worshiping the Son. Which form of Deuteronomy 32:43 does it match?
test.why: The line matches the Greek Septuagint; a Dead Sea Scrolls copy has a similar Hebrew line.

test.q: In Revelation 22:8-9, why does the angel refuse John's worship?
choices: He wants to be called by name
He is not allowed to speak
He is a fellow servant, and worship belongs to God
John has not yet been cleansed
test.why: The angel calls himself John's fellow servant and says, "worship God."

test.q: Stephen, Paul and the writer of Hebrews all say the law was given with the help of whom?
test.why: Acts 7:53, Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2 all speak of angels at the giving of the law.

test.q: Which statement about Colossians 2:18 is accurate?
choices: Scholars read its phrase worship of angels in two main ways
test.why: The phrase may mean worship given to angels or joining in the angels' own worship.

test.q: In the birth stories, how does the angel speak to Joseph?
test.why: Matthew 1:20, 2:13 and 2:19 describe the angel speaking to Joseph in dreams.

test.q: Which reading of the empty-tomb accounts fits them together into one fuller story?
test.why: Harmonizing combines the Gospel accounts into one story and explains differences as different focus.

test.q: Which popular idea did Heiser show is not biblical?
choices: People become angels when they die
test.why: Heiser stressed that the Bible keeps angels and humans distinct. The dead do not become angels.

write.prompt: Are angels in the Bible to be honored as God's servants, or worshiped? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Isaiah 6:1-8, Revelation 22:8-9, Colossians 2:18 or Tobit 12:15-18. Explain what each text says and how Heiser and other readers have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you cite.
Attribute each reading: Heiser argues, many Christians read, other scholars think.
Use the unit's terms, such as mal'ak, elohim, fellowservant and Septuagint.
Compare the readings fairly instead of judging which tradition is right.
Keep what the text says separate from what later art or tradition added.
